sourceEvidence.excerpt: 11.6 — Hallucination: Why It Makes Things Up You've probably experienced this: you ask an AI to recommend a book, and it gives you a title, an author, a publication year, even a one-paragraph summary. It sounds perfect. You search for it and the book doesn't exist. The author is real. The topic is real. The title is plausible. But the book was never written. The model didn't lie to you — it has no concept of lying. It produced the most plausible-sounding next tokens given the pattern of your question. And "plausible-sounding" is the problem. Hallucination is when the model generates text that sounds confident and factual but isn't true — fake citations, invented statistics, wrong dates, fabricated quotes. Not errors from confusion. Confidently stated fictions that read exactly like correct answers. Why it happens (mechanically): The model generates the most probable next token at each step, based on patterns in its training data. It doesn't have a "truth database" to check against. It doesn't know the difference between "a pattern that generates true statements" and "a pattern that generates plausible-sounding statements." When you ask about a topic where the model's training data contains strong patterns — "What is the capital of France?" — it reliably produces correct answers because the correct answer dominates the pattern. When you ask about something more obscure, more nuanced, or in a format that invites specific details (like "list three academic papers about X") — the model generates what that type of output should look like based on patterns. Paper titles, author names, journal names, years — all generated to match the pattern of "what a citation looks like." But the specific combination wasn't verified against reality. It was pattern-completed. When hallucination is most likely: Requests for specific details (names, dates, citations, statistics) Topics with less representation in training data Requests that demand an answer even when the model is uncertain Long-form generation where each token compounds potential errors How it's being addressed (2026): RAG (grounding in retrieved documents reduces hallucination significantly) Chain-of-thought reasoning (models that "think step by step" hallucinate less on reasoning tasks) Citation/source linking (models trained to cite their sources, so outputs can be verified) Confidence calibration (research into
